Ezekiel 1.summary: Among the exiles by the Chebar, Ezekiel sees a storm cloud, four living creatures, wheels moving with them, and a radiant throne-like figure above an expanse (Ezekiel 1:4-25). He falls facedown at the sight of the LORD's glory, careful throughout to describe it only in the language of likeness and appearance (Ezekiel 1:26-28).
Ezekiel 1.whereWeAre: Lamentations closed the exile's grief with an unresolved question rather than a settled answer. Ezekiel opens among the same exiles in Babylon with something different: a priest-prophet's overwhelming vision of God's own throne-chariot, moving freely even far from Jerusalem's temple. Chapter 2 continues directly from this vision, as the voice from the throne commissions Ezekiel to speak to a rebellious people.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: A priest among the exiles by the Chebar, overwhelmed and falling facedown at the sight of the LORD's glory in this opening vision (1:1, 1:28).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Appears above the throne-like vision in fire and brightness, disclosed only through careful language of likeness and appearance (1:26-28).

keyFigures.name: four living creatures
keyFigures.role: Each with four faces and four wings, moving the wheeled chariot-throne wherever the Spirit directs (1:5-12, 1:20).

keyThemes.explanation: God's throne-chariot appears in Babylon, far from Jerusalem's temple, insisting from the book's very first page that God's presence is not confined to one city or building (1:1, 1:28).
Piling up phrases like 'the likeness of' and 'the appearance of' keeps Ezekiel from claiming to describe God directly, treating the vision as something language can only approach (1:5, 1:26-28).
Falling facedown is Ezekiel's only possible response to this vision, modeling the posture any true encounter with God's glory actually produces (1:28).

Ezekiel 2.summary: The divine voice addresses Ezekiel as 'son of man,' lifts him by the Spirit, and sends him to a stubborn and rebellious Israel regardless of how they respond (Ezekiel 2:1-7). A hand presents him with a scroll written on both sides with lamentation and woe, which he must receive before he can speak it (Ezekiel 2:8-10).
Ezekiel 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Ezekiel facedown before the vision of the LORD's glory. Here that same glory speaks, naming Ezekiel 'son of man' and sending him to a stubborn house of Israel regardless of how they respond, then handing him a scroll filled with lamentation. Chapter 3 continues this commissioning scene as Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll before he can speak it.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Addressed as 'son of man,' raised by the Spirit, and sent to a rebellious Israel regardless of how they respond (2:1-5).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Commissions Ezekiel to speak and hands him a scroll of lamentation, mourning, and woe to receive before he can proclaim it (2:3-4, 2:9-10).

keyFigures.name: house of Israel
keyFigures.role: The stubborn, rebellious audience Ezekiel must confront whether or not they actually listen (2:4-7).

keyThemes.explanation: Being renamed 'son of man' and lifted by the Spirit marks Ezekiel's call as something God initiates entirely, not a role Ezekiel sought for himself (2:1-3).
Being warned in advance that the house of Israel is 'impudent and hardhearted' prepares Ezekiel to keep speaking even when his message is rejected (2:4, 2:7).
A scroll written on both sides with only lamentation, mourning, and woe shows that Ezekiel's commission is to deliver bad news in full, not a partial or softened version of it (2:9-10).

Ezekiel 3.summary: Ezekiel eats the scroll and finds it sweet as honey, then is carried to the exiles at Tel-abib, where he sits stunned among them for seven days (Ezekiel 3:1-15). God appoints him a watchman accountable for warning both the wicked and the righteous, then restricts his speech except when God opens his mouth (Ezekiel 3:16-27).
Ezekiel 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with a scroll of lamentation held out to Ezekiel. Here he eats it, finds it sweet, and is carried to the exiles at Tel-abib, where God appoints him a watchman responsible for warning both the wicked and the righteous. Chapter 4 turns from this commissioning to Ezekiel's first enacted sign, a model siege of Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Eats the scroll, finds it sweet, and sits stunned among the exiles at Tel-abib for seven days before taking up his watchman's duty (3:1-3, 3:15).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Appoints Ezekiel a watchman accountable for warning both the wicked and the righteous, then restricts his speech to divinely given words (3:17, 3:26-27).

keyFigures.name: exiles at Tel-abib
keyFigures.role: The community Ezekiel joins and sits among in silence before he begins to speak God's warnings to them (3:15).

keyThemes.explanation: Eating the scroll before speaking it means Ezekiel must absorb God's word personally before he can ever deliver it to others (3:1-3).
Being told that a wicked man's blood will be required at Ezekiel's own hand if he fails to warn him ties the watchman's duty directly to real consequences for silence (3:18-19).
God's control over when Ezekiel's mouth opens and closes shows that even the timing of prophetic speech belongs to God, not the prophet's own discretion (3:26-27).

Ezekiel 4.summary: Ezekiel is told to draw Jerusalem on a clay brick and enact a siege against it, then lie on his sides for a set number of days representing Israel's and Judah's years of guilt (Ezekiel 4:1-8). He receives rationed food and water as a sign of famine, and after he protests the fuel he is told to use, God permits cow dung instead of human waste (Ezekiel 4:9-17).
Ezekiel 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 commissioned Ezekiel as a watchman responsible to warn. Here he begins acting out that warning instead of merely speaking it: drawing Jerusalem on a clay tile, lying on his side for a measured number of days, and eating siege rations, each detail dramatizing the coming hardship. Chapter 5 continues this sign-act with Ezekiel shaving his head and dividing the hair to picture Jerusalem's threefold fate.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Draws Jerusalem on a clay brick, enacts its siege, and lies on his sides for the measured years of Israel's and Judah's guilt (4:1-8).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Instructs each detail of the sign, including the rationed food, and grants Ezekiel's request to use cow dung instead of human waste for fuel (4:9-15).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The city whose coming siege is acted out in miniature through Ezekiel's drawn map and model siege works (4:1-3).

keyFigures.name: Israel and Judah
keyFigures.role: Both kingdoms whose accumulated years of guilt are symbolized by the number of days Ezekiel lies on each side (4:4-6).

keyThemes.explanation: A clay brick, a drawn siege, and an iron pan turn an abstract future threat into something the exiles can actually watch unfold in miniature (4:1-3).
Lying on his side for a day per year of guilt makes Ezekiel physically carry, in a small way, the weight of sin the nation has accumulated over decades (4:4-6).
Rationed food cooked over unclean fuel previews exactly what daily survival will look like under siege and in exile (4:9-13).

Ezekiel 5.summary: Ezekiel shaves his head and beard and divides the hair by burning, striking, and scattering it, acting out Jerusalem's coming fate even though the city sits at the center of the nations (Ezekiel 5:1-5). A small remnant is preserved symbolically in his robe, though even some of those hairs are burned, showing judgment reaching nearly everyone (Ezekiel 5:3-4, 5:12-17).
Ezekiel 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 pictured the coming siege through food rationed by weight. Here Ezekiel shaves his head and beard and divides the hair by burning, striking, and scattering it, acting out how Jerusalem's population will be consumed, killed, and scattered because of persistent disobedience. Chapter 6 turns from this citywide sign to a specific oracle against the hilltop shrines across the whole land.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Shaves his own head and beard and divides the hair by burning, striking, and scattering it to act out Jerusalem's threefold fate (5:1-4).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Explains that Jerusalem, set at the center of the nations, is condemned for disobedience worse than the nations around it (5:5-9).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem's inhabitants
keyFigures.role: The population whose death by plague, sword, and scattering is dramatized directly through Ezekiel's divided hair (5:12).

keyThemes.explanation: Burning, striking, and scattering the hair in three equal parts turns a single sign-act into three distinct, parallel pictures of the city's coming fate (5:1-2).
Naming Jerusalem as a city set deliberately 'in the midst of the nations' makes its coming judgment feel like a particularly public failure of a particularly visible calling (5:5-6).
Threatening that parents will eat their own children ties the siege's horror directly to the covenant curses Israel's own law had already warned about (5:10).

Ezekiel 6.summary: Ezekiel prophesies against the mountains of Israel, where the high places and idols that invited judgment will themselves be destroyed (Ezekiel 6:1-7). The oracle repeats that the people will know the LORD through this judgment, while a remnant scattered among the nations will remember and grieve their unfaithfulness (Ezekiel 6:8-14).
Ezekiel 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 dramatized Jerusalem's coming judgment through divided hair. Here the oracle widens to the mountains of Israel themselves, where the high places and idols that invited judgment will be destroyed along with their worshipers. Chapter 7 presses the same urgency further, announcing that 'the end' has now arrived for the whole land.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Prophesies against the mountains of Israel, condemning the high places and idols that have invited this judgment (6:1-3).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Promises to destroy every illicit altar across the land so that 'ye shall know that I am the LORD' (6:3-7).

keyFigures.name: Israelite worshipers
keyFigures.role: Those who have burned incense to idols on the mountains and hills now condemned for it (6:4, 6:13).

keyFigures.name: survivors among the nations
keyFigures.role: A remnant scattered in exile who will remember and grieve their own unfaithfulness after judgment falls (6:8-10).

keyThemes.explanation: Destroying altars 'in all your dwellingplaces' makes clear that this judgment targets a specific religious practice, not an abstract moral failing (6:3-6).
Survivors scattered among the nations are promised they will remember and loathe themselves for their unfaithfulness, turning exile itself into a delayed form of self-recognition (6:9).
The repeated refrain 'ye shall know that I am the LORD' treats judgment itself as a way God makes himself known, not only mercy or blessing (6:7, 6:14).

Ezekiel 7.summary: A sequence of urgent announcements declares that the end has come upon the land, reaching the four corners of Israel at once (Ezekiel 7:1-9). Wealth, weapons, commerce, and even established religious and political authority cannot avert the coming devastation, which again closes with the promise that the people will know the LORD (Ezekiel 7:10-27).
Ezekiel 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 condemned the idolatrous shrines on Israel's mountains. Here the message sharpens into urgent, repeated announcements that the end has come: wealth, weapons, trade, and even priests and elders will all fail to avert the disaster. Chapter 8 shifts from this general announcement to a specific vision of exactly what is happening inside Jerusalem's own temple.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Announces repeatedly that 'an end is come' upon the whole land, with no escape through wealth or strength (7:2-9).

keyFigures.name: inhabitants of the land
keyFigures.role: Addressed directly as the target of a judgment reaching every corner of their territory at once (7:2, 7:7).

keyFigures.name: king and prince
keyFigures.role: Named among the leaders whose authority will collapse along with everyone else's (7:27).

keyFigures.name: priests and elders
keyFigures.role: Left unable to give any direction or counsel once the disaster actually arrives (7:26).

keyThemes.explanation: Four short, overlapping announcements that 'the end is come' create a mounting sense that there is no more time left to respond (7:2-6).
Silver and gold being thrown into the streets because they cannot buy safety overturns the ordinary assumption that money can solve any crisis (7:19).
Priests, elders, and the king all losing their normal roles at once shows judgment reaching the structures people usually rely on, not just individuals (7:26-27).

Ezekiel 8.summary: In a vision dated to the sixth year of exile, Ezekiel is carried to Jerusalem's temple and shown the image provoking jealousy at its gate and elders burning incense to painted creatures inside (Ezekiel 8:1-13). He also sees women mourning the god Tammuz and men facing east to bow to the sun, each scene exposing a different form of temple-centered unfaithfulness (Ezekiel 8:14-18).
Ezekiel 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 announced that the end had come for the whole land. Here a vision carries Ezekiel to Jerusalem's temple itself and shows him the idolatry actually taking place there: an image provoking jealousy, elders burning incense to carved figures, women weeping for Tammuz, and men bowing to the sun. Chapter 9 continues this same temple vision as judgment begins to fall on what Ezekiel has just seen.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Carried in vision from his own house to Jerusalem's temple, where he is shown exactly what idolatry is taking place there (8:1-3).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Guides Ezekiel through the temple, naming each abomination in turn and asking if he has seen anything worse yet (8:6, 8:15, 8:17).

keyFigures.name: Jaazaniah son of Shaphan
keyFigures.role: An elder leading seventy others in burning incense to painted creatures, despite his family's earlier faithfulness (8:11).

keyFigures.name: seventy elders
keyFigures.role: Caught in the vision burning incense to idols in a hidden chamber, assuming God cannot see them there (8:11-12).

keyFigures.name: women mourning Tammuz
keyFigures.role: Weep at the temple gate for a Mesopotamian god, one more form of worship displacing the LORD (8:14).

keyFigures.name: men in the inner court
keyFigures.role: Twenty-five men who turn their backs on the temple to bow toward the rising sun instead (8:16).

keyThemes.explanation: An idol called 'the image of jealousy' standing at the very gate of God's own house names idolatry as something that directly provokes God rather than merely disappointing him (8:3-5).
Elders burning incense in a dark, private chamber, assuming 'the LORD seeth us not,' are shown in full view of the very God they thought was absent (8:7-12).
Each worse abomination God reveals, ending with men bowing to the sun with their backs to his temple, builds toward the justification for the judgment about to fall (8:17-18).

Ezekiel 9.summary: A visionary command summons agents of judgment: a man in linen marks the foreheads of those who grieve over the city's abominations, while others are sent to strike down everyone left unmarked, beginning at the sanctuary itself (Ezekiel 9:1-7). Ezekiel intercedes for the people, but the LORD answers that their guilt is severe, and the marking agent reports that the task is finished (Ezekiel 9:8-11).
Ezekiel 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 showed Ezekiel the hidden idolatry inside Jerusalem's temple. Here judgment begins to fall on it: a man in linen marks those who grieve over the city's sins, while others are sent to strike down everyone left unmarked, starting at the sanctuary itself. Chapter 10 continues this vision as the glory of the LORD begins to leave the temple it has just judged.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Intercedes for the people when he sees the scale of the coming slaughter, asking if God will destroy the whole remnant of Israel (9:8).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Orders judgment to begin at the sanctuary itself, declaring that the land's guilt and bloodshed are too great to overlook (9:5-10).

keyFigures.name: man clothed in linen
keyFigures.role: Marks the foreheads of everyone who grieves over the city's abominations before the slaughter begins (9:3-4).

keyFigures.name: six armed men
keyFigures.role: Sent through the city to strike down everyone left without the protective mark (9:2, 9:5-7).

keyFigures.name: grieving residents
keyFigures.role: The only people in the vision spared, marked specifically because they sigh and that cry over Jerusalem's sins (9:4, 9:6).

keyThemes.explanation: Marking only those who 'sigh and that cry' for Jerusalem's sins draws a sharp line between the grieving and the indifferent before judgment falls on either group (9:4).
Being told to spare no one, 'neither have ye pity,' confirms that this judgment applies even to the elderly and children, not just active wrongdoers (9:5-6).
Ezekiel's cry, 'wilt thou destroy all the residue of Israel,' shows a prophet who delivers hard warnings while still pleading for mercy underneath them (9:8).

Ezekiel 10.summary: Ezekiel watches burning coals taken from among the cherubim and scattered over the city, then recognizes these same throne-creatures as the living creatures of his first vision by the Chebar (Ezekiel 10:1-15). The glory of the LORD rises from the temple threshold and moves toward the east gate, carried by the same wheeled chariot-throne (Ezekiel 10:16-22).
Ezekiel 10.whereWeAre: Chapter 9 ended with judgment carried out inside the temple itself. Here the glory of the LORD begins to depart: coals are scattered from among the cherubim toward the city, and the glory moves from the temple threshold toward the east gate, carried by the same wheeled creatures Ezekiel saw at the Chebar. Chapter 11 continues this departure as the glory leaves the city entirely.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Recognizes the throne-creatures of this vision as the same living creatures he saw by the Chebar in chapter 1 (10:15, 10:20).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: His glory rises from the temple threshold and moves toward the east gate, beginning its departure from the city (10:4, 10:18-19).

keyFigures.name: man clothed in linen
keyFigures.role: Takes burning coals from among the cherubim and scatters them over the city as a sign of judgment (10:2, 10:6-7).

keyFigures.name: cherubim
keyFigures.role: Identified here by name for the first time, the same throne-attendants Ezekiel first described only as living creatures (10:15, 10:20-22).

keyThemes.explanation: Coals scattered from among the cherubim turn the temple itself into the source of the fire about to consume the city (10:2, 10:6-7).
Recognizing the cherubim as the living creatures of chapter 1 ties this new vision back to Ezekiel's original call, confirming it is the same God acting consistently (10:15, 10:20).
The glory moving by stages, from the cherub to the threshold to the east gate, pictures God's withdrawal as gradual and reluctant rather than sudden or careless (10:18-19).

Ezekiel 11.summary: Ezekiel sees twenty-five officials at the temple's eastern gate giving destructive counsel and trusting a proverb that compares the city to a pot protecting them like meat (Ezekiel 11:1-4). He prophesies against them, Pelatiah dies within the vision itself, and Ezekiel cries out on behalf of the remnant God still promises to gather and give a new heart (Ezekiel 11:5-21). The glory of the LORD departs the city entirely, resting on the mountain to its east (Ezekiel 11:22-23).
Ezekiel 11.whereWeAre: Chapter 10 showed the glory of the LORD moving to the temple's east gate. Here it leaves the city altogether, resting on the mountain to the east, even as Ezekiel confronts officials who give destructive counsel and God promises the scattered exiles a new heart and a future gathering. Chapter 12 turns from this vision of departure to Ezekiel acting out the exile that caused it.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Prophesies against the officials he sees, then cries out in fear that God intends to destroy the whole remnant of Israel (11:4, 11:13).

keyFigures.name: Jaazaniah son of Azzur
keyFigures.role: One of twenty-five officials at the east gate giving wicked counsel that the city is a safe pot and they are the protected meat inside (11:1-3).

keyFigures.name: Pelatiah son of Benaiah
keyFigures.role: Dies suddenly within the vision itself while Ezekiel is still prophesying against the officials (11:13).

keyFigures.name: exiles
keyFigures.role: Promised a little sanctuary in their scattered lands and, eventually, a new heart and spirit to replace a heart of stone (11:16, 11:19).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Judges the officials' false security and promises the scattered exiles both a future gathering and inner renewal (11:7-12, 11:17-20).

keyThemes.explanation: Trusting the proverb that the city is a safe pot protecting them like meat gives the officials false confidence right up until God overturns that very image (11:3, 11:7).
Promising the exiles 'a little sanctuary' in the very countries that scattered them turns displacement itself into a place where God's presence can still be found (11:16).
Promising to remove 'the stony heart' and give 'an heart of flesh' names the real obstacle to obedience as something internal, not merely a lack of information or law (11:19-20).

Ezekiel 12.summary: Ezekiel packs exile baggage and digs through a wall at dusk with his face covered, acting out a ruler's attempted escape and capture (Ezekiel 12:1-16). A second sign depicts anxious, trembling meals eaten under siege, and two popular sayings used to dismiss his warnings as either untrustworthy or far off in the future are both firmly rejected (Ezekiel 12:17-28).
Ezekiel 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 promised the scattered exiles a future gathering even as God's glory departed Jerusalem. Here Ezekiel acts out that scattering in advance: packing exile baggage and digging through a wall at dusk to picture the city's ruler fleeing and being captured, while a second sign pictures the anxious, trembling meals of people under siege. Chapter 13 turns to the false prophets who kept promising that none of this would happen.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Packs exile baggage and digs through a wall at dusk with his face covered, acting out a ruler's attempted escape (12:3-6).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Explains that the sign points to Zedekiah, who will be captured yet never see the land he is taken to (12:10-13).

keyFigures.name: prince in Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The unnamed ruler whose capture and blindness are foretold through Ezekiel's sign, matching Zedekiah's actual fate (12:12-13).

keyFigures.name: rebellious house of Israel
keyFigures.role: Dismisses Ezekiel's warnings with proverbs claiming visions fail or point only to a distant future, both of which God rejects (12:22, 12:27).

keyThemes.explanation: Carrying baggage and digging through a wall turns Ezekiel's own body into the sign his words alone could not make vivid enough (12:3-7).

Eating bread 'with quaking' and knowing the people will one day eat 'with carefulness, and drink their water with astonishment' shows how even routine daily meals will carry the weight of dread under siege (12:18-19).
Rejecting both the claim that visions fail and the claim that they only concern a distant future refuses to let people use either excuse to keep ignoring the warning (12:22-23, 12:27-28).

Ezekiel 13.summary: The LORD denounces prophets who follow their own invented spirit, announce peace with no real foundation, and whitewash Jerusalem's crumbling defenses instead of repairing them (Ezekiel 13:1-16). Women who practice divination through magic bands and veils are condemned in the same breath for ensnaring and exploiting people's fear (Ezekiel 13:17-23).
Ezekiel 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 dramatized the coming exile and dismissed the excuses people used to postpone believing it. Here Ezekiel confronts the false prophets and prophetesses directly, condemning those who announce peace with no word from God and whitewash a crumbling wall instead of repairing it. Chapter 14 turns from public false prophecy to the private idolatry some of Israel's own elders still carry in their hearts.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers God's condemnation of prophets and prophetesses who mislead the people with invented claims of peace (13:1-2).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Compares false prophets to builders whitewashing a weak wall, declaring that his own storm will bring it down regardless (13:10-14).

keyFigures.name: false prophets
keyFigures.role: Follow their own spirit and 'have seen nothing,' yet claim to speak a word the LORD never gave them (13:3, 13:6).

keyFigures.name: women practicing divination
keyFigures.role: Use magic bands and veils to ensnare people for handfuls of barley and pieces of bread (13:18-19).

keyThemes.explanation: Asking whether a prophet's word actually came from 'the mouth of the LORD' gives hearers a concrete standard for telling true prophecy from invented claims (13:2-3).
Promising peace 'and there was no peace' names the specific danger of comfort offered without any real basis behind it (13:10).
Hunting souls 'for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread' ties false divination directly to greed, not just spiritual error (13:19).

Ezekiel 14.summary: Elders come to consult Ezekiel while secretly holding idols in their hearts, and God refuses to let them combine false worship with a claim on his guidance (Ezekiel 14:1-11). Even if Noah, Daniel, and Job themselves lived in such a land, their righteousness could save only their own lives, not the nation around them, and survivors will later help the exiles understand just how deserved this disaster was (Ezekiel 14:12-23).
Ezekiel 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 condemned prophets who offered false reassurance instead of real warning. Here some of Israel's elders come to Ezekiel for guidance while secretly holding idols in their hearts, and God tells them that even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves, not a nation determined to sin. Chapter 15 turns to a short parable making a similar point about Jerusalem's own uselessness apart from faithfulness.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Consulted by elders who come to him while secretly keeping idols in their hearts (14:1, 14:3).

keyFigures.name: elders of Israel
keyFigures.role: Visiting petitioners whose hidden idolatry disqualifies their inquiry before Ezekiel even answers them (14:3-4).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Refuses to let hidden idolatry coexist with a claim on his guidance, and names Noah, Daniel, and Job as men who could save only themselves (14:7-8, 14:14).

keyFigures.name: Noah, Daniel, and Job
keyFigures.role: Three famous righteous men cited as proof that even the most exceptional personal righteousness cannot save a whole unfaithful nation (14:14, 14:20).

keyThemes.explanation: Elders who keep idols in their hearts while consulting God's true prophet reveal that outward religious behavior can mask a genuinely divided loyalty (14:3-4).
Saying that Noah, Daniel, and Job could deliver only themselves, not even their own sons or daughters, insists that individual righteousness has real but limited reach (14:14, 14:16).
Promising that survivors will later explain their own conduct to the exiles turns the disaster itself into evidence meant to help people finally understand why it happened (14:22-23).

Ezekiel 15.summary: The LORD compares Jerusalem to the wood of a vine, which is not even useful for making a simple peg, let alone building anything sturdy (Ezekiel 15:1-5). If a whole, healthy vine has no practical worth, a vine already scorched by fire has even less, and Jerusalem's unfaithfulness is about to bring exactly that kind of devastation (Ezekiel 15:6-8).
Ezekiel 15.whereWeAre: Chapter 14 insisted that not even the most righteous individuals could save a persistently unfaithful nation. Here a short parable compares Jerusalem to the wood of a vine, which is useless for anything but fuel even when whole, and worse once it has already been burned. Chapter 16 expands this same charge of uselessness into the book's longest and most detailed allegory of Jerusalem's unfaithfulness.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Compares Jerusalem to vinewood, useless for any craft even before it is burned, let alone after (15:1-5).

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Receives this short parable as a direct explanation of why Jerusalem's unfaithfulness leads to devastation (15:6-8).

keyFigures.name: inhabitants of Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Likened to vine wood already scorched at both ends, with no practical use left to argue for sparing them (15:4-6).

keyThemes.explanation: Comparing Jerusalem to vine wood, not timber, insists the city's whole identity was meant to be fruit-bearing, and it has nothing else to fall back on once that purpose fails (15:2-3).
A vine already burned at both ends having even less value than a whole one pictures judgment as something that removes any remaining excuse for mercy (15:4-5).
Calling the coming devastation a direct result of 'trespassing grievously' refuses to treat Jerusalem's ruin as random misfortune (15:8).

Ezekiel 16.summary: A sustained allegory pictures Jerusalem as an abandoned infant whom the LORD rescues, raises, and marries, adorning her with jewels and fine clothing (Ezekiel 16:1-14). The city repays that care with idolatry and foreign alliances, becoming more blameworthy than her symbolic sisters Samaria and Sodom (Ezekiel 16:15-52). Even so, judgment is followed by a promise that God will remember his covenant with her from the days of her youth (Ezekiel 16:59-63).
Ezekiel 16.whereWeAre: Chapter 15 compared Jerusalem to worthless, half-burned vine wood. Here a sustained allegory tells Jerusalem's whole history as the story of an abandoned infant whom the LORD rescues, raises, and marries, only to have her repay that care with idolatry and foreign alliances worse than her neighbors Samaria and Sodom. Chapter 17 turns from this personal allegory to a political riddle about Judah's last kings.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Rescues, raises, and marries the abandoned infant Jerusalem in this allegory, then still promises to remember his covenant with her despite her betrayal (16:6-14, 16:60).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Personified as an unfaithful wife who repays rescue and marriage with idolatry, foreign alliances, and even child sacrifice (16:15-21, 16:28-29).

keyFigures.name: Samaria and Sodom
keyFigures.role: Jerusalem's personified sisters, used to show that her own unfaithfulness has outdone even their proverbial sins (16:46-51).

keyThemes.explanation: Finding an abandoned infant 'polluted in thine own blood' and simply commanding her to live grounds Jerusalem's whole existence in an act of unearned rescue (16:5-6).
Using gifts God gave her, her own jewels and fine clothing, to make idols turns Jerusalem's unfaithfulness into a betrayal using the very blessings meant to honor the relationship (16:17).
Promising to remember the covenant 'in the days of thy youth' even after everything that followed shows God's commitment outlasting the relationship's worst failures (16:60).

Ezekiel 17.summary: A riddle of two great eagles and a cedar sprig is explained as Babylon's deportation of Jehoiachin and Zedekiah's broken oath in appealing to Egypt for help instead (Ezekiel 17:1-21). The LORD declares that breaking a sworn political oath carries real consequences, even when it was sworn to a foreign king (Ezekiel 17:16-19). The closing image answers this collapse with a tender shoot God himself plants, promising a future tree exalted above every other (Ezekiel 17:22-24).
Ezekiel 17.whereWeAre: Chapter 16 ended with a promise that God would remember his covenant despite Jerusalem's unfaithfulness. Here a riddle of two eagles and a cedar retells that same unfaithfulness in political terms: Zedekiah's broken oath to Babylon and his doomed appeal to Egypt, before the chapter closes with a very different planting, a tender shoot God himself sets to grow into a future tree. Chapter 18 turns from this national riddle to a direct dispute over whether individuals suffer for their parents' guilt.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Tells and then explains the riddle of two eagles and a cedar sprig to a people who may not otherwise grasp its political meaning (17:2, 17:11-12).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Interprets the riddle as Judah's recent history and promises a future shoot he himself will plant into an exalted tree (17:19-24).

keyFigures.name: king of Babylon
keyFigures.role: The first eagle in the riddle, who carries off Jehoiachin and installs Zedekiah as a bound vassal king (17:3-4, 17:12-13).

keyFigures.name: king of Judah
keyFigures.role: Zedekiah, who breaks his sworn oath of loyalty to Babylon by turning instead to Egypt for help (17:15-18).

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh of Egypt
keyFigures.role: The second eagle, appealed to for military aid that the riddle predicts will not actually save Zedekiah (17:7, 17:17).

keyThemes.explanation: Treating Zedekiah's broken oath to Babylon as a direct offense against God, since it was sworn in his name, makes political loyalty a matter of covenant faithfulness (17:18-19).
Turning to 'Pharaoh with his mighty army' for help that the riddle predicts will fail exposes reliance on Egypt as a repeated, almost predictable mistake (17:15, 17:17).
God's own hand planting a tender shoot into 'a goodly cedar' answers the chapter's political collapse with a future entirely of God's own making (17:22-23).

Ezekiel 18.summary: The exiles' proverb blaming their fathers for their own suffering, 'the fathers have eaten sour grapes,' is rejected as an explanation for individual guilt (Ezekiel 18:1-4). The chapter compares the conduct of righteous and wicked parents and children across generations to insist that each person is judged by their own actions (Ezekiel 18:5-20). It closes calling Israel to turn from its transgressions and receive a new heart, since God takes no pleasure in anyone's death (Ezekiel 18:21-32).
Ezekiel 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 closed with a promise of future hope planted by God's own hand. Here that hope requires a correction first: the exiles' proverb blaming their fathers for their own suffering is rejected, as God insists each person is judged by their own conduct and that even a lifelong sinner who turns can live. Chapter 19 turns from this teaching on individual responsibility to a lament for the fallen royal house as a whole.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Rejects the exiles' proverb blaming their fathers, insisting that each person is judged for their own conduct, and that even a lifelong sinner who turns can live (18:1-4, 18:21-23).

keyFigures.name: house of Israel
keyFigures.role: Disputes God's justice directly, prompting the extended teaching on personal responsibility that answers their complaint (18:2, 18:25, 18:29).

keyFigures.name: righteous and wicked parents and children
keyFigures.role: Hypothetical examples walked through case by case to show that guilt and righteousness do not simply pass down a family line (18:5-18).

keyThemes.explanation: Declaring that 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die' and not the child for the parent's sin rejects any idea that guilt simply transfers down a family line (18:20).
Promising that none of a repentant sinner's past transgressions will be remembered insists that a changed life, not a clean record, is what actually matters (18:21-22).
Ending with 'turn yourselves, and live ye' makes the whole chapter's teaching into an invitation, not just a legal clarification (18:32).

Ezekiel 19.summary: A lament compares Judah's royal mother to a lioness whose cubs, one after another, are captured and led away in chains to Egypt and Babylon (Ezekiel 19:1-9). The image then shifts to a once-fruitful vine, transplanted in good soil but now uprooted, withered, and burned, left without any strong branch fit to rule (Ezekiel 19:10-14).
Ezekiel 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 insisted that each person answers for their own conduct, not their ancestors'. Here that principle plays out in Judah's own royal history: a lament compares the nation's mother to a lioness whose cubs, her princes, are captured one by one, and then to a once-fruitful vine now uprooted and burned. Chapter 20 turns from this lament to a much longer review of the rebellion that led to this royal collapse.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers this lament for Judah's fallen royal house in the same breath he has just finished reviewing its leaders' failures (19:1).

keyFigures.name: princes of Israel
keyFigures.role: Mourned here as captured lion cubs, including Jehoahaz taken to Egypt and Jehoiachin taken to Babylon (19:3-4, 19:9).

keyFigures.name: mother lioness and vine
keyFigures.role: Two shifting images for the royal house itself, first a lioness whose cubs are captured, then a vine uprooted and burned (19:2, 19:10-14).

keyThemes.explanation: Comparing Judah's kings to lion cubs trained to hunt and then caught in a pit pictures royal power turned destructive before it is finally captured (19:3-4, 19:6-8).
A vine's 'strong rods' being plucked, withered, and burned pictures Judah's own royal authority as something that has simply run out (19:12, 19:14).
Calling this chapter a lament, framed by that word at its start and end, gives grief its own legitimate place in facing national collapse (19:1, 19:14).

Ezekiel 20.summary: When elders come to inquire of him, Ezekiel recounts Israel's repeated rebellions in Egypt, the wilderness, and the land, each time met with divine restraint shown only for the sake of God's own name (Ezekiel 20:1-26). The oracle rejects the people's present idolatry outright, yet still promises a future gathering, purification, and worship offered on God's holy mountain (Ezekiel 20:33-44). A brief, puzzling parable of fire consuming the southern forest closes the chapter in many English editions (Ezekiel 20:45-49).
Ezekiel 20.whereWeAre: Chapter 19 lamented Judah's royal house as captured lion cubs and a burned vine. Here, when elders come to inquire of him, Ezekiel reviews that same collapse at much greater length, tracing Israel's rebellion back through Egypt and the wilderness even as God's patience, for his own name's sake, kept the nation from being destroyed outright. Chapter 21 turns from this historical review to a sword song naming Jerusalem's judgment directly.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Recounts Israel's history of rebellion at length when elders come to inquire of him, though God first refuses to be inquired of at all (20:1, 20:3).

keyFigures.name: elders of Israel
keyFigures.role: Come seeking a word from God, only to receive a history of rebellion rather than the answer they may have wanted (20:1-3).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Reviews Egypt, the wilderness, and the land as three repeated cycles of rebellion met each time by restraint for his own name's sake (20:8-9, 20:13-14, 20:21-22).

keyFigures.name: Israelites across generations
keyFigures.role: Each generation shown repeating its ancestors' idolatry, extending guilt from the exodus all the way to Ezekiel's own hearers (20:18, 20:30-31).

keyThemes.explanation: Walking through Egypt, the wilderness, and the land as three separate cycles of rebellion shows Israel's unfaithfulness was not a single lapse but a sustained pattern (20:8, 20:13, 20:21).
Repeating 'I wrought for my name's sake' after each cycle credits God's own reputation, not Israel's merit, for the nation surviving this long (20:9, 20:14, 20:22).
Promising to accept Israel's worship again only after gathering and purging it insists that restored worship must be genuinely cleansed, not merely resumed (20:40-41).

Ezekiel 21.summary: The LORD announces a sword sharpened and polished against Jerusalem and the whole land, and Ezekiel performs mourning gestures to match its coming grief (Ezekiel 21:1-17). A sign portrays the king of Babylon standing at a fork in the road, using divination to decide between attacking Rabbah of Ammon or Jerusalem, with the answer falling on Jerusalem (Ezekiel 21:18-23). Judah's own ruler is told his crown will be removed until the one with rightful claim to it comes, and a separate, final oracle addresses the Ammonites directly (Ezekiel 21:25-32).
Ezekiel 21.whereWeAre: Chapter 20 traced Israel's long history of rebellion and God's patient restraint. Here that restraint runs out: a sharpened sword is announced against Jerusalem, Ezekiel acts out mourning gestures, and Babylon's king is pictured choosing by divination which city, Jerusalem or Rabbah, to attack first. Chapter 22 widens the sword's target from Jerusalem's coming siege to a full catalog of the sins that brought it on.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Performs mourning gestures, sighing and groaning before the people, to embody the grief this sword song announces (21:6-7).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Announces a sword sharpened and polished against Jerusalem and declares Judah's crown removed until its rightful owner comes (21:9-10, 21:26-27).

keyFigures.name: king of Babylon
keyFigures.role: Pictured at a literal fork in the road, using divination, arrows, and consulted idols to decide between Rabbah and Jerusalem (21:19-22).

keyFigures.name: prince of Israel
keyFigures.role: Zedekiah, told that his crown and kingdom are being overturned as judgment for persistent wrongdoing (21:25-27).

keyFigures.name: Ammonites
keyFigures.role: Addressed in a separate, closing oracle that extends this same sword imagery beyond Judah alone (21:28-32).

keyThemes.explanation: A sword repeatedly called 'sharpened' and 'furbished' turns Babylon's coming attack into something the text makes almost feel physically present (21:9-10, 21:28).
The king of Babylon using arrows, idols, and a liver to choose his target shows Jerusalem's fate decided by pagan divination rather than any merit of its own (21:21-22).
The threefold cry 'I will overturn, overturn, overturn it' empties Judah's monarchy of authority until the one with rightful claim finally comes (21:27).

Ezekiel 22.summary: The LORD catalogs Jerusalem's violence, corrupt leadership, and exploitation of foreigners, orphans, and widows, comparing the whole city to impure metal melted down in a furnace (Ezekiel 22:1-22). Prophets, priests, officials, and ordinary people are all named as implicated, and God says he can find no one willing to stand in the breach and defend the land (Ezekiel 22:23-31).
Ezekiel 22.whereWeAre: Chapter 21 pictured Babylon's king choosing Jerusalem as his target by divination. Here the LORD catalogs exactly why: violence, corrupt leadership, exploitation of the vulnerable, and profaned worship fill the city, pictured as impure metal with no one left willing to stand in the gap to defend it. Chapter 23 returns to allegory to retell this same unfaithfulness through the story of two sisters.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Catalogs Jerusalem's violence, corrupt leadership, and sexual violations, and says he can find no one willing to stand in the breach for the land (22:2-12, 22:30).

keyFigures.name: princes, priests, prophets, and people
keyFigures.role: Every level of Jerusalem's society named as complicit in the city's collapse, with no group exempted from blame (22:25-29).

keyFigures.name: foreigners, orphans, and widows
keyFigures.role: Specifically named among the vulnerable people Jerusalem's leaders and residents have wronged and oppressed (22:7, 22:29).

keyThemes.explanation: Listing bloodshed, oppression of foreigners, and abuse of the fatherless together treats Jerusalem's violence and its social injustice as the same underlying problem (22:6-7).
Comparing Jerusalem to dross left in a furnace means the city has already failed the test that was supposed to purify it (22:18-19).
Naming princes, priests, prophets, and people in one unbroken list of accusation refuses to let any single group escape responsibility for the city's condition (22:25-29).

Ezekiel 23.summary: Samaria and Jerusalem are portrayed as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, whose illicit relationships with Assyria and Babylon symbolize idol worship and reckless political dependence (Ezekiel 23:1-21). Their conduct brings a humiliating judgment carried out by the very powers they once courted, and the chapter's final exhortation demands an end to this kind of unfaithfulness altogether (Ezekiel 23:22-49).
Ezekiel 23.whereWeAre: Chapter 22 cataloged Jerusalem's sins directly, name by name. Here the same unfaithfulness returns in allegory: Samaria and Jerusalem appear as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, whose reckless political and religious entanglements with Assyria and Babylon bring the judgment already announced. Chapter 24 moves from this allegory to the dated moment the judgment actually begins.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Narrates this allegory of two unfaithful sisters and pronounces the judgment their conduct has earned (23:22-35).

keyFigures.name: Oholah (Samaria)
keyFigures.role: Personifies the northern kingdom's earlier political and religious entanglement with Assyria, ending in its own destruction (23:5-10).

keyFigures.name: Oholibah (Jerusalem)
keyFigures.role: Personifies Jerusalem's even worse entanglement with Assyria and then Babylon, outdoing her sister's unfaithfulness (23:11-21).

keyFigures.name: Assyrians and Babylonians
keyFigures.role: The foreign powers both sisters pursue as lovers in the allegory, later turned into their executioners (23:9, 23:22-24).

keyThemes.explanation: Giving both sisters' political alliances the language of sexual unfaithfulness treats foreign dependence as a betrayal of the same depth as religious infidelity (23:5-9, 23:11-14).
Reminding Jerusalem that Samaria already fell for this same behavior removes any excuse that Jerusalem could not have seen this outcome coming (23:9-11).
Ending with a demand that 'all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness' turns this one allegory into a warning meant for a much wider audience (23:48-49).

Ezekiel 24.summary: In a dated oracle marking the start of Babylon's siege, Ezekiel compares Jerusalem to a boiling pot whose contents and built-up corrosion cannot be cleansed by any ordinary means (Ezekiel 24:1-14). His own wife dies that same day, and he is commanded not to perform any customary public mourning, becoming himself a sign of how stunned and silent the survivors will be when the sanctuary falls (Ezekiel 24:15-27).
Ezekiel 24.whereWeAre: Chapter 23 pictured Jerusalem's entanglements with foreign powers as a sister's reckless unfaithfulness. Here the judgment those entanglements invited finally arrives: on the very day Babylon's siege begins, Ezekiel compares Jerusalem to a boiling, uncleansable pot, and his own wife's sudden death becomes a sign of the stunned grief still ahead. Chapter 25 turns outward from Jerusalem's own fall to the neighboring nations who will mock it.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Compares Jerusalem to a boiling, uncleansable pot on the very day Babylon's siege begins, then loses his own wife that same evening (24:1-6, 24:18).

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel's wife
keyFigures.role: Dies suddenly and without any public mourning allowed, her unnamed loss becoming a sign of the city's coming grief (24:16-18).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Explains that Ezekiel's silence in grief previews the exiles' own stunned, wordless reaction when the temple falls (24:19-24).

keyFigures.name: exiles
keyFigures.role: Told that they, like Ezekiel, will waste away in their sins rather than mourn normally when news of the temple's loss reaches them (24:23-24).

keyThemes.explanation: Being told to write down the exact date Babylon's siege began ties this whole chapter to a specific, verifiable moment rather than a vague future threat (24:1-2).
Losing 'the desire of thine eyes' in his own wife's death makes Ezekiel's message cost him something no listener could mistake for a mere rhetorical device (24:16, 24:18).
Being forbidden the normal signs of grief turns Ezekiel's unnatural composure into the sign itself, previewing a shock too deep for ordinary mourning (24:16-17, 24:22-23).

Ezekiel 25.summary: The LORD announces judgment against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia in turn, each one held accountable for mockery, contempt, vengeance, or lasting hostility toward Judah's fall (Ezekiel 25:1-17). Each oracle treats the neighboring nation's own response to Judah's calamity, not just its past history, as the direct basis for its coming judgment (Ezekiel 25:6, 25:12, 25:15).
Ezekiel 25.whereWeAre: Chapter 24 marked the day Babylon's siege of Jerusalem began. Here the book turns to Judah's neighbors, Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia, each judged for mocking or exploiting Jerusalem's fall rather than grieving with her. Chapter 26 continues this sequence of oracles against the nations with a much longer judgment on Tyre.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers four short oracles against Judah's immediate neighbors in a single connected sequence (25:1-17).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Judges each nation specifically for how it responded to Judah's calamity, not simply for being a foreign people (25:3, 25:6, 25:8, 25:12, 25:15).

keyFigures.name: Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, and Philistines
keyFigures.role: Four neighboring peoples condemned in turn for mockery, contempt, vengeance, or lasting hostility toward fallen Judah (25:3, 25:8, 25:12, 25:15).

keyThemes.explanation: Ammon's open mockery, 'Aha,' at the temple's fall is condemned as a specific offense, not just an unfriendly attitude toward a weakened neighbor (25:3).
Moab's claim that Judah is 'like unto all the heathen' is answered by judgment that treats Judah's God-given distinctiveness as still very much real (25:8-9).
Edom and Philistia taking personal revenge 'with a despiteful heart' are judged for acting as their own avengers rather than leaving judgment to God (25:12, 25:15).

Ezekiel 26.summary: A dated oracle condemns Tyre for celebrating Jerusalem's fall as an opportunity for its own commercial gain (Ezekiel 26:1-6). It predicts a prolonged assault, ruined walls, and total commercial collapse, naming Nebuchadnezzar as the attacking king whose armies will carry out the judgment (Ezekiel 26:7-14). The oracle's imagery culminates in Tyre's descent into the depths, mourned by the very nations that once traded with it (Ezekiel 26:15-21).
Ezekiel 26.whereWeAre: Chapter 25 pronounced shorter judgments on four of Judah's neighbors. Here a longer, dated oracle turns to Tyre, condemned for profiting from Jerusalem's ruin and now facing a prolonged siege, ruined walls, and a commercial collapse pictured as a descent into the depths. Chapter 27 continues this same judgment on Tyre with an extended lament over its lost splendor.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers this dated oracle announcing Tyre's coming destruction in unusually specific, drawn-out detail (26:1-2).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Promises to bring many nations against Tyre 'as the sea causeth his waves to come up' and to scrape the city bare (26:3-5).

keyFigures.name: Tyre
keyFigures.role: A Phoenician trading city condemned for celebrating Jerusalem's fall as an opportunity for its own profit (26:2).

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
keyFigures.role: Named directly as the king whose armies and siege works will carry out this judgment against Tyre (26:7-11).

keyThemes.explanation: Tyre's plan to profit commercially from Jerusalem's destruction, 'I shall be replenished,' is treated as its own distinct offense, separate from any direct hostility (26:2).
Nebuchadnezzar's siege engines and horsemen are described in enough physical detail to make Tyre's coming destruction feel like a real military campaign, not just poetic threat (26:7-11).
Tyre's trading wealth, the very thing that made it proud, provides no defense at all once the siege actually begins (26:12-14).

Ezekiel 27.summary: A long lament pictures Tyre as a richly built merchant ship, constructed and supplied by materials and workers drawn from many different nations (Ezekiel 27:1-11). Its extensive trade network and long list of trading partners and commodities build a portrait of commercial splendor reaching from Tarshish to Arabia (Ezekiel 27:12-25). That splendor is then abruptly overturned when the ship sinks in the heart of the seas, and every trading nation mourns its loss (Ezekiel 27:26-36).
Ezekiel 27.whereWeAre: Chapter 26 announced Tyre's coming destruction and descent into the depths. Here a long lament pictures exactly what will be lost: Tyre as a magnificent merchant ship, built and supplied by nations across the known world, suddenly wrecked while its trading partners mourn from the shore. Chapter 28 turns from Tyre's commercial fall to the personal pride of its ruler.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Sings this extended funeral lament over Tyre's wrecked trading empire (27:2, 27:32).

keyFigures.name: Tyre
keyFigures.role: Pictured as a magnificently built merchant ship, supplied by craftsmen and goods from many nations, now sinking in the sea (27:3-9, 27:26-27).

keyFigures.name: mariners and merchants
keyFigures.role: The sailors, pilots, and caulkers who build and sail Tyre's ship-like economy, left to mourn when it finally sinks (27:27-29).

keyFigures.name: trading nations
keyFigures.role: Dozens of partners named by name, from Tarshish to Arabia, each supplying some part of Tyre's now-lost wealth (27:12-24).

keyThemes.explanation: Tyre's hull, mast, oars, and sails each sourced from a different nation shows a single city's wealth depending on a whole network of other peoples (27:5-7).
A list running from Tarshish's silver to Sheba's spices maps Tyre's reach across the entire known world in a single catalog (27:12-24).
All that accumulated cargo sinking 'in the midst of the seas' in a single moment shows how quickly even vast, diversified wealth can be lost (27:27, 27:34).

Ezekiel 28.summary: The ruler of Tyre is condemned for claiming divine status, a claim the LORD answers bluntly by insisting that he is a man and not God despite his wealth (Ezekiel 28:1-10). A second, more exalted lament for the king of Tyre uses Edenic and cherubic imagery to portray his original splendor and his downfall through pride and violence (Ezekiel 28:11-19). The oracle then turns briefly against neighboring Sidon before ending with a promise that Israel will finally dwell securely once its hostile neighbors are judged (Ezekiel 28:20-26).
Ezekiel 28.whereWeAre: Chapter 27 lamented Tyre's wrecked trading network. Here the oracle turns to Tyre's own ruler, condemned for claiming to be a god despite being mortal, and to its king, pictured in Edenic, cherub-like splendor before his fall, followed by a brief judgment on neighboring Sidon and a promise that Israel will finally dwell securely. Chapter 29 turns from these Phoenician cities to Egypt, the last and largest nation addressed in this sequence.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers both the oracle against Tyre's ruler and the lament for its king, then turns briefly to Sidon (28:2, 28:12, 28:21).

keyFigures.name: prince and king of Tyre
keyFigures.role: Addressed in two related speeches: first condemned for claiming to be a god, then lamented in Edenic, cherub-like language describing a fall from original splendor (28:2, 28:12-17).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Answers Tyre's claim to divinity bluntly, 'yet thou art a man, and not God,' and promises Israel secure dwelling once its hostile neighbors are judged (28:9, 28:24-26).

keyFigures.name: Sidon
keyFigures.role: A neighboring Phoenician city given a brief, separate judgment after the much longer oracle against Tyre (28:21-23).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Promised a secure, thorn-free homeland once the surrounding nations that despised it have themselves been judged (28:24-26).

keyThemes.explanation: The ruler's claim 'I am a God' is answered simply by pointing out that he will die like any other man, 'the deaths of them that are slain' (28:2, 28:8).
Describing the king of Tyre with language of Eden and cherubic splendor before his fall gives his pride a cosmic scale that the earlier oracle's plainer accusation did not (28:13-17).
Promising Israel a homeland with 'no more a pricking brier' only after judging Tyre and Sidon ties Israel's safety directly to its neighbors finally facing consequences (28:24-26).

Ezekiel 29.summary: A dated oracle portrays Pharaoh as a great river creature in the Nile, claiming the river as his own creation and property (Ezekiel 29:1-6). Egypt will be humbled for having failed as a reliable support to Israel, pictured as a reed staff that splinters and wounds the hand of anyone who leans on it, though a limited restoration is announced after forty years (Ezekiel 29:6-16). A later-dated oracle assigns Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as his reward for an exhausting, unrewarded campaign against Tyre (Ezekiel 29:17-20).
Ezekiel 29.whereWeAre: Chapter 28 closed its Phoenician oracles with a promise of secure dwelling for Israel. Here the oracles against the nations turn to Egypt: Pharaoh is pictured as a great river-creature claiming the Nile as his own, judged for failing Israel as a reliable ally, though a limited restoration is promised after forty years. Chapter 30 continues this judgment on Egypt, naming the day of the LORD that will fall on it and its allies.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers both the dated oracle against Pharaoh as the great river-creature and the later oracle assigning Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar (29:1-3, 29:17-18).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Judges Egypt for claiming the Nile as its own and for failing Israel as a reliable source of support (29:3, 29:6-7).

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh king of Egypt
keyFigures.role: Pictured as a great dragon in the Nile, confident in his own power, about to be dragged out and cast into the open field (29:3-5).

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
keyFigures.role: Given Egypt as compensation for his long, costly, and otherwise unrewarded siege of Tyre (29:18-20).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Egypt's former ally, whose unreliable support from Egypt is named as part of the reason for Egypt's own judgment (29:6-7, 29:16).

keyThemes.explanation: Pharaoh's boast that 'my river is mine own, and I have made it for myself' exposes a ruler who credits himself for what is simply a natural feature of his land (29:3, 29:9).
Egypt described as a reed staff that would 'break, and rend all their shoulder' pictures the real physical harm caused by leaning on an unreliable ally (29:6-7).
Promising Egypt's return after forty years, but only as 'the basest of the kingdoms,' lets restoration and permanent diminishment coexist in the same prophecy (29:13-15).

Ezekiel 30.summary: The day of the LORD is announced as disaster for Egypt and every nation allied with it, with cities, idols, and military strength all set to fall together (Ezekiel 30:1-19). A dated oracle pictures Pharaoh's arm broken beyond healing even as Babylon's arm grows stronger by comparison (Ezekiel 30:20-26).
Ezekiel 30.whereWeAre: Chapter 29 pictured Pharaoh as a boastful river-creature about to be judged. Here that judgment is named outright as a day of the LORD: Egypt's cities, idols, and military strength will all fail together, with Pharaoh's own arm broken even as Babylon's arm grows strong. Chapter 31 continues this same Egyptian judgment through the image of a once-towering cedar cut down.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Announces the day of the LORD against Egypt and all the nations allied with it in a single sweeping oracle (30:2-5).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Declares that Egypt's cities, idols, and military strength will all fall together, with Pharaoh's own arm broken beyond recovery (30:13, 30:21-22).

keyFigures.name: Egyptians and their allies
keyFigures.role: Named alongside Egypt's own cities, listed one after another as sharing in its coming downfall (30:4-9).

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: The specific target of a dated oracle in which his strong arm, a symbol of royal power, is broken so he can no longer hold a sword (30:21-25).

keyFigures.name: king of Babylon
keyFigures.role: The ruler whose own arm God strengthens even as Pharaoh's is broken, carrying out this judgment on Egypt (30:24-25).

keyThemes.explanation: Naming Cush, Put, Lud, and other allies alongside Egypt shows that joining a doomed power's alliance does not grant any exemption from its judgment (30:4-5).
Listing Egypt's cities and idols one after another, each set to fall in turn, treats the whole religious and civic infrastructure as equally vulnerable (30:13, 30:17-18).
Breaking Pharaoh's arm so that 'it shall not be bound up to be healed' pictures a disabling, not merely a temporary, loss of strength (30:21).

Ezekiel 31.summary: Pharaoh and all his multitude are addressed through the image of Assyria as an unmatched cedar, watered by deep springs and admired by every tree and nation around it (Ezekiel 31:1-9). That very splendor leads to pride, and the cedar is felled and sent down among the dead, a direct warning that Egypt's own grandeur offers no more immunity from judgment (Ezekiel 31:10-18).
Ezekiel 31.whereWeAre: Chapter 30 announced a day of the LORD breaking Pharaoh's strength. Here Egypt is warned through the example of Assyria, pictured as an unmatched cedar watered by deep streams and admired by every nation, whose very splendor led to pride, felling, and a descent among the dead. Chapter 32 closes this long sequence of Egyptian oracles with two final laments for Pharaoh himself.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Addresses Pharaoh and all his multitude through the extended image of Assyria as a towering, unmatched cedar (31:2-3).

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh and his multitude
keyFigures.role: The direct audience for this warning, told that Egypt's own splendor will end exactly as Assyria's did (31:2, 31:18).

keyFigures.name: Assyria
keyFigures.role: Pictured as a cedar of Lebanon watered by deep springs and envied by every tree in Eden, until its pride brings it down (31:3-9, 31:10-14).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Explains that Assyria's felling is a warning for Egypt, since no nation's grandeur can protect it from the same judgment (31:10-11, 31:18).

keyThemes.explanation: Even 'the cedars in the garden of God could not hide him' describes a tree so magnificent that nothing in Eden itself could compare, making its fall land even harder (31:8-9).
The cedar's height making 'his heart is lifted up in his height' ties the very splendor God gave it to the pride that brought it down (31:10).
Sending the fallen cedar down 'with the trees of Eden' to comfort others already cut down pictures imperial collapse as something every great power eventually shares (31:16, 31:18).

Ezekiel 32.summary: A lament portrays Pharaoh as a great sea creature, once thrashing through the waters, now caught in a net and cast out to rot in the open field (Ezekiel 32:1-10). A second lament sends Egypt down to join Assyria, Elam, and other fallen nations already lying among the uncircumcised dead, each one once feared and now equally powerless (Ezekiel 32:11-32).
Ezekiel 32.whereWeAre: Chapter 31 warned Egypt through Assyria's own fall from towering cedar to felled corpse. Here two laments complete the sequence: Pharaoh is pictured as a sea creature finally caught and cast aside, and then as one more fallen power joining Assyria, Elam, and others already lying in the realm of the dead. Chapter 33 turns from these oracles against foreign nations back to Ezekiel's own responsibility as a watchman to his people.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Sings two separate laments for Pharaoh, first as a caught sea creature and then as a fallen power among the dead (32:2, 32:18).

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Compared to a young lion and a sea monster, confident in his own strength until he is caught, cast out, and left to rot (32:2-6).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends Egypt down to the pit to lie among already-fallen nations as a final, deliberate humiliation (32:18-21).

keyFigures.name: Assyria, Elam, Meshech-Tubal, Edom, and Sidonians
keyFigures.role: Nations already lying in the realm of the dead, named one by one as Egypt is shown joining them there too (32:22-30).

keyThemes.explanation: Comparing Pharaoh to a young lion and then a trapped sea monster shows raw strength proving useless once judgment actually arrives (32:2-3).
Covering the sun, moon, and stars when Egypt falls uses cosmic imagery to mark a loss the text treats as significant on more than a merely local scale (32:7-8).
Placing Egypt among 'the uncircumcised' already lying dead alongside Assyria and Elam insists that no empire's past glory earns it a different end from any other (32:19, 32:24-25).

Ezekiel 33.summary: Ezekiel is again compared to a watchman responsible for warning his people, and God declares that he takes no pleasure in anyone's death, only in their repentance (Ezekiel 33:1-11). A fugitive finally arrives from Jerusalem reporting, 'the city is smitten,' and Ezekiel's own mouth is opened at last (Ezekiel 33:21-22). He challenges survivors who claim the land by right while still sinning, and exiles who enjoy his words like a pleasant song without ever doing what they hear (Ezekiel 33:23-33).
Ezekiel 33.whereWeAre: Chapter 32 closed the long sequence of oracles against the nations with Egypt's descent among the already-fallen. Here the book turns back to Judah itself: Ezekiel's watchman role is renewed, a fugitive finally arrives with news that Jerusalem has fallen, and Ezekiel challenges survivors who claim the land by right and exiles who enjoy his words without ever acting on them. Chapter 34 turns from these failed hearers to the failed leaders, Israel's own shepherds, who let this happen.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Has his watchman role renewed, then is finally able to speak freely once news of Jerusalem's fall reaches him (33:7, 33:21-22).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Declares he takes no pleasure in anyone's death, holds Ezekiel accountable for warning people honestly, and insists that hearing his words without doing them accomplishes nothing (33:11, 33:30-32).

keyFigures.name: fugitive from Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Arrives among the exiles with the long-awaited news, 'the city is smitten,' confirming everything Ezekiel had warned (33:21).

keyFigures.name: survivors in the ruins
keyFigures.role: Claim a right to the land by citing Abraham's example, even while continuing in the very practices that brought judgment (33:24-26).

keyFigures.name: exile community
keyFigures.role: Listens to Ezekiel's words as pleasant entertainment, 'a very lovely song,' without ever acting on what they hear (33:31-32).

keyThemes.explanation: The watchman who fails to warn being held responsible for a death he could have prevented ties Ezekiel's own responsibility directly to the lives of his hearers (33:6, 33:8).

Insisting that a wicked man who turns from sin will live, and a righteous man who turns to sin will die, keeps present conduct, not past record, as the real basis for life or death (33:14-16, 33:18-19).
Enjoying Ezekiel's words 'as a very lovely song' while never acting on them exposes a response that mistakes aesthetic pleasure for actual obedience (33:32).

Ezekiel 34.summary: Israel's shepherds, its own leaders, are accused of feeding themselves rather than tending the weak, injured, and scattered sheep entrusted to them (Ezekiel 34:1-10). God promises to search for and rescue the flock himself, judging between fat and lean sheep, and to appoint 'my servant David' as the one true shepherd under an everlasting covenant of peace (Ezekiel 34:11-31).
Ezekiel 34.whereWeAre: Chapter 33 showed exiles who heard Ezekiel's words without doing them. Here their leaders come under the same kind of scrutiny: Israel's shepherds are condemned for feeding themselves instead of the flock, and God promises to seek out the scattered sheep himself and set 'my servant David' over them as one true shepherd under a covenant of peace. Chapter 35 turns from this promise for Israel to a judgment on the neighbor who gloated over its scattering.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers this double message condemning Israel's failed leaders and announcing their replacement by God himself (34:1-2).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Promises to search for and rescue the scattered flock personally and to set 'my servant David' over it as one true shepherd (34:11, 34:23).

keyFigures.name: shepherds of Israel
keyFigures.role: Condemned for feeding themselves, ruling 'with force and with cruelty,' and leaving the flock scattered and exposed (34:2-5).

keyFigures.name: sheep of the flock
keyFigures.role: Israel's own ordinary people, described as weak, injured, and scattered under the care of failed leaders (34:4, 34:16).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named as the one shepherd God will set over the restored flock, ruling under an everlasting covenant of peace (34:23-25).

keyThemes.explanation: Listing exactly what good shepherds should do, strengthen the weak and heal the sick, by name shows precisely what Israel's actual leaders failed to provide (34:4).
God himself promising to 'search my sheep, and seek them out' steps into the gap left by shepherds who abandoned that very job (34:11-12).
Naming the coming ruler 'my servant David' ties this future hope directly back to the dynasty Israel's own history had already placed its hope in (34:23-24).

Ezekiel 35.summary: A prophecy against Mount Seir accuses Edom of lasting hostility and open rejoicing over Israel's ruin and desolation (Ezekiel 35:1-10). Edom's claim that Israel's abandoned territories now belong to it is flatly rejected, and the same desolation it wished on Israel is announced for its own land instead (Ezekiel 35:11-15).
Ezekiel 35.whereWeAre: Chapter 34 promised Israel a true shepherd after its own leaders' failure. Here that promise finds its necessary counterpart in judgment on Edom, condemned under the name Mount Seir for its lasting hostility and for claiming Israel's desolated territory as its own. Chapter 36 turns back to that same territory, Israel's own mountains, now promised restoration rather than loss.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers this oracle against Mount Seir directly after the preceding promises of restoration for Israel (35:1-2).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Condemns Edom's 'perpetual hatred' and rejects outright its claim on Israel's now-desolate land (35:5, 35:10).

keyFigures.name: Mount Seir (Edom)
keyFigures.role: Judah's longtime rival, condemned by name for rejoicing at Israel's fall and claiming its abandoned territory (35:2-3, 35:10).

keyFigures.name: Israelites
keyFigures.role: The people whose desolation Edom celebrated and whose land Edom tried to claim as its own (35:5, 35:12).

keyThemes.explanation: Calling Edom's hatred 'perpetual' or 'old' ties this specific judgment to a conflict with a long, unbroken history rather than a single recent offense (35:5).
Edom's plan to take over 'these two nations and these two countries' after Israel's fall treats someone else's catastrophe as a real estate opportunity (35:10).
Promising Edom the exact desolation it wished on Israel applies the measure Edom used against someone else right back onto Edom itself (35:14-15).

Ezekiel 36.summary: God addresses Israel's own mountains directly with promises of renewed fertility, resettlement, and the removal of the shame they have carried among the nations (Ezekiel 36:1-15). This restoration is explicitly for the sake of God's own name, not Israel's merit, and includes cleansing, a new heart, and a new spirit that will finally enable renewed obedience (Ezekiel 36:22-27). The land itself will become so fruitful that onlookers will compare it to the garden of Eden (Ezekiel 36:33-38).
Ezekiel 36.whereWeAre: Chapter 35 condemned Edom for claiming Israel's desolated land. Here Israel's own mountains receive the opposite promise: renewed fertility and resettlement, pursued not for Israel's own merit but for the sake of God's name, culminating in the promise of a new heart and a new spirit that will finally make obedience possible. Chapter 37 pictures that same renewal even more dramatically, as a valley of dry bones comes back to life.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Speaks directly to the mountains of Israel, promising them renewed fruitfulness after their long reproach among the nations (36:1, 36:8-9).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Restores Israel for the sake of his own name, promising cleansing, a new heart, and a new spirit that will finally make obedience possible (36:22-27).

keyFigures.name: mountains of Israel
keyFigures.role: Personified as the land itself, addressed directly and promised cultivation, population, and freedom from further mockery (36:1, 36:33-34).

keyFigures.name: house of Israel
keyFigures.role: The displaced people this whole restoration is for, promised cleansing from their past idolatry and shame (36:17, 36:25, 36:31-32).

keyFigures.name: surrounding nations
keyFigures.role: Watch Israel's restoration and are expected to recognize that the LORD himself has rebuilt what was ruined (36:36).

keyThemes.explanation: Promising that the mountains will be 'tilled and sown' again answers the earlier oracle's destruction of those same mountains with their eventual restoration (36:9, 36:34).
Promising to 'take away the stony heart' and give 'an heart of flesh' names the real problem as an inability to respond, not a lack of instruction (36:26).
Repeating 'not for your sakes' before describing Israel's restoration forecloses any later claim that the nation somehow earned its own renewal (36:22, 36:32).

Ezekiel 37.summary: Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones given flesh, breath, and life again, explained as hope for the whole house of Israel even in the depths of exile (Ezekiel 37:1-14). He then joins two sticks representing Judah and Joseph into one, symbolizing a reunited nation under a single Davidic ruler and an everlasting covenant of peace (Ezekiel 37:15-28).
Ezekiel 37.whereWeAre: Chapter 36 promised a new heart and spirit for a renewed Israel. Here that same renewal is pictured as dead bones brought back to life in a valley, a sign of hope for the whole house of Israel, followed by two sticks joined into one to show Judah and Joseph reunited under a single Davidic shepherd and an everlasting covenant. Chapter 38 turns from this picture of secure, reunited peace to one final, large-scale threat against it.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Prophesies to a valley of dry bones until they live, then joins two sticks to picture a reunited Israel and Judah (37:7, 37:17).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives breath and life to the dry bones as a sign of hope for all of exiled Israel, and promises an everlasting covenant under one Davidic ruler (37:12-14, 37:26).

keyFigures.name: whole house of Israel
keyFigures.role: Identified directly with the dry bones, a people who feel as hopeless and lifeless as a battlefield's unburied dead (37:11).

keyFigures.name: Judah and Joseph (Ephraim)
keyFigures.role: The two formerly divided kingdoms, represented by two sticks that become one in Ezekiel's hand (37:16-19).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named as the single king who will rule the reunited nation forever under this new, everlasting covenant (37:24-25).

keyThemes.explanation: Describing the bones as 'very dry' before anything happens insists the hope that follows begins from genuine, not exaggerated, hopelessness (37:2, 37:11).
Two sticks becoming one in Ezekiel's own hand turns a centuries-old political split between Israel and Judah into something visibly, physically undone (37:17, 37:19).
Calling this covenant 'everlasting' and placing God's own sanctuary 'in the midst of them for evermore' makes the promised unity permanent rather than provisional (37:26, 37:28).

Ezekiel 38.summary: Gog of the land of Magog, leading Meshech, Tubal, and a wide coalition of distant peoples, is summoned against a restored Israel living securely without walls (Ezekiel 38:1-13). The oracle declares in advance that this invader will be defeated amid earthquake and confusion, so that the nations will recognize God's holiness through his defeat (Ezekiel 38:14-23).
Ezekiel 38.whereWeAre: Chapter 37 pictured Israel reunited and secure under one shepherd and an everlasting covenant. Here that very security draws a massive final threat: Gog of Magog, leading a coalition of distant peoples, is summoned against restored Israel, though the chapter already announces his defeat as proof of God's holiness before the nations. Chapter 39 completes this same battle, describing Gog's actual destruction and its lingering aftermath.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.role: Delivers this prophecy against Gog before the attack it describes ever takes place, already announcing its outcome (38:3, 38:18).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Draws Gog into this attack specifically so that the nations will know his holiness through Gog's defeat (38:16, 38:23).

keyFigures.name: Gog of Magog
keyFigures.role: A coalition leader drawn against restored Israel's peaceful, unwalled villages, pictured as a storm rolling in to cover the land (38:2, 38:9, 38:16).

keyFigures.name: Meshech, Tubal, Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, and Beth-togarmah
keyFigures.role: Distant peoples named as Gog's allies in this massive, final-looking coalition (38:5-6).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: The restored, securely dwelling people this entire coalition is drawn together to attack (38:8, 38:11-12).

keyThemes.explanation: Gog's coalition specifically targets a people already living securely without walls, aiming at the very peace the earlier chapters promised (38:8, 38:11).
An earthquake, confusion among the attackers, and weapons turned against each other defeat Gog without Israel itself ever needing to fight (38:19-21).
Stating the purpose outright, 'that the heathen may know me,' makes Gog's defeat a demonstration of God's holiness before a watching world, not just a military outcome (38:16, 38:23).

Ezekiel 39.summary: The judgment against Gog continues as his invading forces are destroyed on the mountains of Israel, their weapons burned for fuel and their dead buried in a lengthy, deliberate cleansing of the land (Ezekiel 39:1-16).
